02 / ASSUMPTIONS, IN THE OPEN

Three coherent futures

These are starting hypotheses. Change them above and the whole forecast responds.

Starter ceiling assumptions: 120/year is about two flights per week; 1,500/year is about four per day; 10,000/year is about 27 per day, before operating availability. All cases assume sustained program funding and a market for the modeled flights. Program cancellation, prolonged fleet-wide grounding, and demand collapse sit outside this scenario range.

04 / HOW TO READ THIS MODEL

Evidence anchors the rate. Assumptions set the future.

The model, without a black box

A logistic curve describes the potential flight rate. Its learning rate equals Falcon 9’s fitted rate multiplied by the selected acceleration. A delay shifts the start of the ramp.

Potential = K / [1 + (K / r₀ − 1)e−k·t]
Flights/year = availability × min(potential, fleet × 365.25 / turnaround)

Here K is the long-run annual ceiling; r₀ is the starting annualized rate; t is years after the selected delay. The ceiling bundles infrastructure, licenses, and demand. Fleet and turnaround transition geometrically to the January 1, 2036 targets. Annual counts integrate the rate across each year.

Two initial vehicle equivalents and Falcon’s 2026 median turnaround are modeling anchors, not a claim that Starship already operates a reusable fleet. Before routine reuse, an equivalent represents production-supported flight capacity. Later it represents the smaller effective capacity of ships and boosters.

What the curves do—and don’t—say

The band spans the minimum and maximum of your three cases. The cases have no assigned probabilities. Calling this a 90% confidence interval would imply evidence we do not have.

The Falcon curves are descriptive nonlinear least-squares fits. Weekly cadence uses complete weeks including zero-launch weeks. The turnaround curve fits complete-quarter medians with at least three measured intervals; the upper plateau is fixed to the first observed reflight interval to stabilize the fit.

Falcon’s fitted plateau is not an engineering limit. Recent launch demand can flatten cadence, and a large fleet can lengthen intervals even when refurbishment gets faster. The model is not causally identified and is not a validated forecast.

Scenario ceilings above today’s reviewed launch rates assume additional pads, environmental reviews, operating licenses, and demand. An environmental review is not an operating license.
